historical_timeline.summary: Heavy drinking in Paris, probably absinthe and wine.
Paul Gauguin joined him at the Yellow House in Arles.
First crisis, with confusion and an injury to his left ear; taken to hospital the next morning.
Discharged from the hospital in Arles.
Readmitted with delirium and hallucinations; admitted again on February 27.

claims.statement: Vincent van Gogh was born on March 30, 1853, and decided to become an artist at the age of 27.

In October 1888 the painter Paul Gauguin joined Van Gogh at the Yellow House in Arles, in the south of France, where Van Gogh hoped to found an artists' community; their discussions about art became more frequent and heated, and the situation deteriorated.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Social context for the crisis. Gauguin appears only in this history; the modern episode names no real person.

claims.statement: On December 23, 1888, when he was 35, after a heated argument, Van Gogh cut off his left ear in a state of utter confusion. The police found him at home the next morning and took him to hospital. He could later recall nothing of what had happened.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic first episode of psychosis and for the history of self-injury during confusion. The record states the documented fact once and repeats no further detail.

claims.statement: In the hospital in Arles he was treated by the assistant physician Dr. Felix Rey. His condition worsened and he spent several days in isolation; he then recovered slowly and went home after about two weeks, on January 7, 1889.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the brief hospital stay in the modern episode and the timing of the index visit soon after discharge.

claims.statement: New attacks followed about a month later. He was admitted to the hospital in Arles again on February 7, 1889, with delirium and hallucinations, and again on February 27, 1889, after neighbours petitioned for him to be confined.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date. Recurrence is why the modern episode treats the first episode as the start of a possibly recurrent illness and plans for early warning signs.

source_links.locator: new attacks just a month later

claims.statement: On May 8, 1889, he had himself admitted voluntarily to the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole psychiatric hospital in Saint-Remy-de-Provence, where he stayed for a year. The director, Dr. Peyron, entered his diagnosis in the admissions register; Nolen and colleagues report that Peyron described attacks of epilepsy separated by long intervals.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date. The asylum physician's diagnosis of epilepsy is why the modern workup includes an EEG and brain MRI.

source_links.locator: attacks of epilepsy, separated by long intervals

claims.statement: In a letter to his brother Theo written at the asylum about May 23, 1889, he wrote that after the shock nothing would have been so agreeable to him as never to wake up again, that this horror of life was already less pronounced and the melancholy less acute, and that other patients, like him, had heard sounds and strange voices during their crises.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own description of a wish not to wake up, of low mood, and of hearing voices during the crises. It anchors the passive death wish recorded, without intent or plan, in the modern safety assessment. Quoted as the Van Gogh Museum quotes the letter.

claims.statement: Further crises began in July 1889, while he was painting a quarry, and the following months alternated between crises and recovery; Nolen and colleagues count four episodes at Saint-Remy between July 1889 and April 1890.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: He drank heavily in Paris from 1886, probably both absinthe and wine, and later wrote to his brother that he had become almost an alcoholic from overdoing it; in Arles he seems to have cut down.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic alcohol use disorder.

source_links.locator: almost an alcoholic as a result of overdoing it

claims.statement: Nolen and colleagues judged that he had an alcohol use disorder, with dependence shown by failed attempts to cut down in Arles, made worse by malnutrition and poor sleep.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; supports treating alcohol use from the first visit.

claims.statement: Nolen and colleagues concluded that he probably had a bipolar mood disorder, more likely bipolar II than bipolar I, with recurrent depressive episodes, some of them psychotic, and probably hypomanic symptoms. The Van Gogh Museum states that no all-embracing diagnosis has been found.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and disputed; one reason the modern diagnosis is provisional with a bipolar disorder in the differential.

source_links.locator: an all-embracing diagnosis is yet to be found

claims.statement: Nolen and colleagues also found strong indications of borderline personality traits, present as an underlying vulnerability from young adulthood.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation from questionnaires completed by art historians; not used as a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: Nolen and colleagues proposed that the brief psychosis after the ear incident was a delirium from alcohol withdrawal, because he was forced to stop drinking suddenly when he was admitted to hospital. The writer Martin Bailey questioned part of their reasoning, arguing that they underestimated how much he went on drinking afterwards.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and disputed; puts alcohol withdrawal in the modern differential.

claims.statement: Nolen and colleagues concluded that focal (temporal lobe) epilepsy, which Dr. Rey had suggested in Arles, cannot be excluded as an additional condition, although its probability cannot be judged without an EEG or brain imaging.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; the reason the modern workup includes an EEG and brain MRI.

claims.statement: Schizophrenia, Meniere's disease, syphilis, acute intermittent porphyria and thujone poisoning from absinthe have also been proposed; Nolen and colleagues judged schizophrenia and the others unlikely or highly unlikely, because he had no psychotic symptoms between episodes and no negative symptoms.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; recorded so that the modern differential is not taken from popular accounts.

claims.statement: He left Saint-Remy in May 1890 for Auvers-sur-Oise, near Paris, where Dr. Paul Gachet was asked to keep an eye on him. He was exceptionally productive there, but felt lonely and depressed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode; recorded as history.

claims.statement: On July 27, 1890, he shot himself in the chest; he died in Auvers-sur-Oise on July 29, 1890, at the age of 37.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, recorded without detail. It is not used in the modern episode, where suicide-risk care follows the guideline for any person after a first episode of psychosis.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Dignified, recovery-oriented primary care for a 35-year-old painter twelve days after discharge from a first psychiatric admission for psychosis with mood features: keeping the diagnosis provisional and stating the differential (bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, brief psychotic or schizophreniform disorder, alcohol withdrawal or alcohol-induced psychosis, and focal epilepsy), a first-episode workup with brain MRI and EEG, antipsychotic monitoring to the APA and ADA/APA standard (weight at every visit, blood pressure, fasting glucose, A1c and lipids at baseline and 12 weeks, akathisia and movement checks with the AIMS), recognizing and treating akathisia, AUDIT-C, PEth and naltrexone for alcohol use disorder, sleep as treatment and as an early warning sign, coordinated specialty care, and a structured safety assessment with lethal-means counseling and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline reviewed at every visit, on the APA 1883 schizophrenia guideline, the CANMAT and ISBD bipolar guidelines, and the CMID depression and bipolar monograph.

referral.question: First episode of psychosis with mood features in a 35-year-old painter, twelve days after discharge from a first psychiatric admission. He takes aripiprazole 10 mg daily, started in hospital, and drinks heavily. Please review the provisional diagnosis and differential, the medication plan, the treatment of his alcohol use, and the workup for seizures, and enroll him in coordinated specialty care
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: For several weeks before the episode he slept three or four hours a night while painting, without feeling tired, and was full of plans, while drinking five or six drinks most days. Just before the episode a fellow painter who shared his house left after a heated argument. He then became acutely confused, with hallucinations and suspiciousness, and injured his left ear himself without suicidal intent; he remembers little of it. In hospital he was treated for alcohol withdrawal and for the ear wound; the confusion cleared over a few days, but hallucinations and suspiciousness lasted longer, and aripiprazole 10 mg and thiamine were started two days before discharge. Today he has no hallucinations by day but hears his name called as he falls asleep; his mood is low (PHQ-9 13, item 9 scored 1 for passive thoughts of not waking up, without intent or plan); a structured safety assessment and safety plan were completed, he has no firearm access, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is in his phone. AUDIT-C 9; he still has two or three drinks most evenings. No personal history of seizures. Results today: white cells 6.8, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, MCV 102 fL, platelets 172; sodium 137, potassium 4.1, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, eGFR 108; fasting glucose 91 mg/dL, A1c 5.3%; total cholesterol 184, LDL 106, HDL 52, triglycerides 130 mg/dL; AST 58, ALT 44, GGT 96 U/L; TSH 1.8 mIU/L; vitamin B12 388 pg/mL; PEth 284 ng/mL. consultant_note.history: Mr. van Gogh, a 35-year-old painter, is seen at the request of Dr. Verhoeven four weeks after aripiprazole 10 mg was started in hospital. He has taken every dose. The confusion of the acute episode has cleared, and he hears nothing by day, but on some nights he hears his name called as he falls asleep and feels briefly that people in the street are talking about him. In the weeks before the episode he slept three or four hours a night, painted almost continuously, and felt full of energy and plans; he was drinking five or six drinks a day, and the confusion began soon after he stopped drinking abruptly. assessment.assessment: The leading possibilities are bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, suggested by weeks of reduced need for sleep and increased activity before the episode and low mood after it, and a psychosis caused by heavy drinking and its abrupt withdrawal, suggested by the timing; the two may have combined. A brief psychotic or schizophreniform disorder remains possible; schizophrenia is less likely with this course. Focal epilepsy is unlikely without seizure-like events but is reasonable to look for once. The diagnosis should stay provisional and be settled by the course: a later manic or depressive episode would point to bipolar disorder, and psychosis without mood change or alcohol to a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder. Aripiprazole is a sound choice for its low metabolic and prolactin effects; the residual night-time symptoms justify a modest increase. A mood stabilizer is not needed now, because aripiprazole also treats mania; lithium would be the first choice if a mood episode occurs
Drinking is the most changeable risk for relapse and for suicide. He takes no opioids, and his liver tests are well below three times the upper limit, so naltrexone is suitable

The injury happened in confusion and without suicidal intent; his current passive thoughts of not waking up are a separate and treatable part of his low mood. His risk is raised in the months after a first episode, and the safety plan is appropriate

recommendations: Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg once daily; if akathisia appears, go back to 10 mg rather than add more medicines, and treat it with propranolol if needed
No mood stabilizer now; consider lithium if a manic or depressive episode occurs
Complete the brain MRI and sleep-deprived EEG; if both are normal and there are no seizure-like events, no further epilepsy testing is needed
Start naltrexone 50 mg daily, continue thiamine, follow drinking with PEth, and treat alcohol and psychosis together in the same team
Enroll him in coordinated specialty care now: care coordination, individual resilience-focused therapy, education for him and the people he chooses, supported return to work, and peer support

Monitor weight at every visit for six months, blood pressure, fasting glucose, A1c and lipids at about 12 weeks and then yearly, akathisia and parkinsonism at each visit early on, and the AIMS every six months
Measure the PHQ-9 at least monthly while he is depressed and review suicide risk at every contact
Treat sleep loss as an early warning sign: regular hours and a plan to call the team after two short nights
Continue the antipsychotic after remission; review the length of treatment with him near the one-year mark, with a written relapse plan before any reduction
